name: Jujube fruit (Ziziphus jujuba)
short: Swallowed pits (stones): oesophageal perforation (case series, mostly older adults) and a child's perforated bowel. Anaphylaxis to related Indian jujube. Trials: mild diarrhoea in 3 of 63 newborns.
text: These data are for the fruit of Ziziphus jujuba, eaten or taken as syrups, extracts or powder by mouth; the sour jujube seed has its own entry. Swallowed pits: a 2026 case report describes an 8-year-old boy whose ileum (small bowel) was perforated by an impacted jujube pit, causing peritonitis and secondary appendicitis that needed emergency surgery; he recovered. Case series describe swallowed jujube pits lodged in the oesophagus (gullet), mostly in older people; the abstracts do not name the jujube species. In a series of 114 consecutive cases over 3 months, titled as in the aged, 4 people had oesophageal perforation, were treated conservatively and none died; the authors describe a high incidence of perforation with this injury. In a series of 40 patients, 30 (75%) of them aged 58 or older, endoscopy found damage to the oesophageal lining in 35 and perforation in 5. In a retrospective review of adults, a pit 25 mm or more across and more than 12 hours between swallowing and presentation were associated with more complications. A case report describes a 62-year-old woman whose oesophagus was perforated through-and-through by a jujube seed; it was retrieved by endoscopy, the perforation was treated with endoscopic clips, and she was discharged well within a few days. These harms were caused by swallowed pits (stones), so they concern the fruit eaten with its stone; none of these abstracts involves syrups or extracts. Allergy: a 2020 case report describes anaphylaxis, treated with epinephrine, in a 55-year-old man after eating Indian jujube (Ziziphus mauritiana), a different species, which he had eaten often since childhood; the authors call it extremely rare in people without latex allergy. In trials: among 63 newborns with jaundice given jujube fruit extract with phototherapy, 3 developed slight diarrhoea after 1 to 2 days, which resolved on its own. In a 3-month randomised trial in children aged 2 to 10 with functional constipation, liver and kidney tests and blood sugar were checked, and side effects were reported only in the polyethylene glycol comparison group (30 children completed on jujube syrup). In a 28-day trial of jujube oxymel (a syrup preparation whose full composition the abstract does not give) with cetirizine in 92 people with chronic urticaria, the authors mention minimal side effects; and in a 12-week placebo-controlled trial of a liquid jujube extract for chronic constipation, 2 of 18 on jujube and 16 of 19 on placebo dropped out because of severe constipation, the condition being treated; the abstract gives no adverse-event data, although the authors call the extract safe. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
